title: Defend a schema and index plan for competing workloads
brief: A multi-department equipment service must show each borrower’s current loans, each item’s history, and a daily cross-department report. Propose the core relational identities and references, defend a small index plan, and explain how you would investigate a slow report without harming the interactive paths. Use L031–034; transaction-isolation deep dives are not required yet.

clarifications.question: Which entities and scope?
clarifications.answer: Each physical item belongs to one department and has a department-unique barcode. Loans refer to physical items and borrowers. A loan has opened_at and optional returned_at.

clarifications.question: What are the main queries?
clarifications.answer: Current loans for a borrower within one department, ordered newest first; full history for one item; a daily aggregate over all departments.

clarifications.question: What sizes and rates?
clarifications.answer: There are five million loan records, 1% active. Interactive current-loan reads occur 100/s; the report runs once daily. One department owns half the history.

clarifications.question: Which invariants?
clarifications.answer: At most one active loan per physical item. Historical loans must remain. Loan-item references must not cross the declared department.

clarifications.question: What slow-path evidence is available?
clarifications.answer: The endpoint fetches 50 loans and then separately fetches each borrower and item description, causing 101 queries. A daily report legitimately scans much of the data.

clarifications.question: What can be approximate?
clarifications.answer: The daily report may finish in minutes; interactive page correctness and tenant isolation remain strict. Exact total-count pagination is not required.

hints: Distinguish a physical item from its model description and the loan’s historical identity.
An active-only uniqueness rule differs from making item_id unique across all history.
Count queries per user action before attributing every delay to one SQL statement.
changes: An engineer proposes one index on every column. Defend a smaller workload-driven choice and its write costs.
The largest department grows tenfold while small tenants stay stable. What plan evidence should be revisited?
referenceSolution: Use stable scoped item and loan IDs, department-unique barcode, composite references for department correctness, and explicit borrower ownership. Preserve historical loans; a unique partial index over (department_id,item_id) WHERE returned_at IS NULL expresses one active loan in this state model. Interactive indexes should align tenant/borrower equality with time/ID order; item history needs its own scoped item/time path if measured frequency justifies it. The daily broad report may reasonably scan rather than use an index for every row. Reduce N+1 with a correctly scoped join for one-to-one fields or bounded batches, preserving parent pagination before any one-to-many expansion. Compare estimates and actual row counts with representative large/small department values, record query count and pool/lock wait, and use safe EXPLAIN ANALYZE practice. Indexes cost writes, space, and cache; all-column indexing is not a plan. No particular planner operator is mandatory without evidence.
debrief: Look for a traceable connection from access pattern to key order, and from invariant to constraint. Do not award points merely for naming indexes. Ask the candidate to explain the 101-query amplification and why a broad report can legitimately scan. Retry with a different active fraction and a changed parent/child relationship.
